opus-5.5.text:
Well, when I started at OpenAI in the summer of 2022, ChatGPT hadn't been released yet, but GPT-3 was around and you could already see where things were heading. When I sat down to think about what I could contribute on the safety side, the most immediate misuses weren't the science-fiction scenarios of an AI taking over the world. They were much more mundane, almost boring. But they were going to hit very soon and affect a lot of people.

The first thing I thought about was academic cheating. If you can ask a language model to write your term paper on the causes of the French Revolution, every student in the world is going to realize that pretty quickly. I'm a professor, so this was close to home. And sure enough, within weeks of ChatGPT coming out, I was getting emails from colleagues and teachers asking, "How do I know if my students wrote this?"

The second was propaganda and disinformation at scale. Before, if you were a state actor or anyone else who wanted to flood social media with posts supporting some position, you needed a troll farm, actual humans typing. Now you could generate endless plausible-sounding posts, each slightly different, each in a different voice, essentially for free.

Then there's spam, phishing, and impersonation, like writing in a specific person's style to fool someone they know.

What all of these have in common is that someone takes AI-generated text and passes it off as human-written. So the question I focused on was attribution: could we make it possible, after the fact, to tell whether a piece of text came from the model? That led to my work on watermarking. The idea is that when the model picks its next token, instead of sampling truly at random, it uses a pseudorandom function keyed with a secret. To a reader, the output looks completely normal, the quality is indistinguishable. But someone holding the key can compute a score over the text, and with a few hundred tokens you can get pretty high statistical confidence that it came from the model.

I should be honest that I didn't foresee everything. I think I underestimated how fast and how widely this would spread, that within a couple of months it would be one of the fastest-adopted consumer products in history. And watermarking has real limitations. Someone who's determined can paraphrase the text, or ask the model to write in a weird way and then undo it. It's not a silver bullet; it raises the cost of the most lazy forms of misuse. There were also real questions about whether one company should deploy it unilaterally if its competitors don't, because then users might just go elsewhere. Those debates were very much alive inside the company.

But broadly, the low-hanging-fruit misuses, cheating, spam, propaganda, impersonation, were pretty foreseeable, and I think anyone who'd thought about it for a while could have predicted them. The question was always what we could do technically to mitigate them.

r001.rationale: He says students would use a language model to write term papers and identifies academic cheating as a foreseeable misuse before ChatGPT’s release.

r002.rationale: He says AI could replace troll farms and generate endless varied posts to flood social media, clearly describing trolling and spam at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, to be honest, I don't think I foresaw very much about ChatGPT specifically, because I don't think anyone at OpenAI really foresaw what it would become. When I joined in the summer of 2022, the model that became ChatGPT was essentially a research artifact. People knew GPT-3 was impressive, but the idea that you'd wrap a chat interface around it and it would get a hundred million users in a couple of months, that wasn't the plan. It was supposed to be a kind of low-key research preview. So the scale of the thing caught everyone off guard, including me.

What I did think about, and what I was actually hired to think about, was a narrower question: once you have a model that can generate fluent text on any topic, how do you tell whether a given piece of text came from the model? The obvious misuse cases were already clear to anyone paying attention. Students using it to write their term papers. Propaganda and disinformation generated at scale. Spam, fake reviews, fake personas on social media. These weren't hard to predict. I think I wrote on my blog around that time that the first thing I'd worry about is not some sci-fi scenario where the AI decides to take over, but just the mundane problem of the internet filling up with text that nobody wrote.

So the project I worked on was watermarking, which is the idea that you bias the model's choice of tokens in a way that's statistically undetectable to a human reader but that leaves a signature you can pick up if you know the secret key. And I was quite excited about that because it turns out to be a nice theoretical computer science problem. You can get a scheme where the quality of the output is essentially unaffected, and yet with a few hundred tokens you can detect the watermark with very high confidence.

Where I was more naive, I'd say, is on the deployment side. I thought if you had a working technical solution, you'd deploy it. But there are all these other considerations. If you watermark and your competitors don't, does that just push users to the competitors? Does watermarking even help if people can paraphrase the output through a different model? Those are the questions that made it a much harder sell internally than I expected, and I think that's a general lesson. The technical piece is often the easy part.

astra-6.text: The obvious concern was that it could make it much cheaper to produce convincing text at scale—spam, phishing messages, propaganda, disinformation. You wouldn’t need someone sitting there writing each message, and you could tailor the messages to different audiences. Those possibilities were foreseeable before release. What was much harder to predict was how people would actually use it, which abuses would become significant, and how well the safeguards would hold up.

sol-6.1.text: Before it was released, I was already worried about people using it to generate misinformation, spam, and phishing messages at a much greater scale. You could see how a system that produces plausible text on demand could make those things cheaper and easier. The difficult question was what we could do about that without undermining all the legitimate uses—whether, for example, there could be some way to recognize text generated by an AI.
